title: Evals, Testing, Errors & Cost
scopeHtml: Scope: the design document, eval grading methods, test levels and tracing, retriable vs terminal errors, tool errors, model routing, cost levers and multi-agent economics.

questions.promptHtml:
Why write the eval before building the feature?

  • A. Evals are required by the API
  • B. It forces you to define success first, so "done" is a score on a fixed set of cases rather than rationalizing whatever the model produced
  • C. It makes the model faster
  • D. It replaces unit tests

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. An eval is dataset + expected behavior + grader + average, and you change one variable at a time so you know what moved the score.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Without an eval, 'done' is a feeling after a few manual tries. The pipeline is small: load cases, run each through the feature, grade each, average. A first score of 2 or 3 out of 10 is normal; what matters is that it rises as you change one thing at a time (prompt, tools or model). It complements unit tests (D); it does not replace them.

questions.promptHtml:
Match the grader. (1) A classifier that must return one of five labels. (2) A feature that must return valid JSON with a required field. (3) A paragraph explaining a recommendation, judged for faithfulness.

  • A. (1) LLM judge, (2) exact match, (3) code check
  • B. (1) exact match, (2) code-graded check, (3) LLM-as-judge
  • C. (1) code check, (2) judge, (3) exact match
  • D. LLM judge for all three

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. One correct form → exact match; structural rule → code check; open-ended quality → judge.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Exact match is cheap but fails valid paraphrases and reorderings. Code checks catch syntax and format failures but say nothing about quality. A judge is the only scalable option for faithfulness but it is costly, noisy, and its numbers mean nothing until calibrated against known-good cases. Run code graders on every commit; schedule the judge for periodic quality passes.

questions.contextHtml: Your prompt tests pass. Your parser unit tests pass. In production, refund requests fail. A trace shows retrieval ok, prompt built ok, model call ok, parse(answer) raises KeyError: amount because the model returned the field under a different name.
questions.promptHtml:
Which test layer was missing, and what would have caught it?

  • A. More unit tests on the parser
  • B. An integration test of the model-output → parser handoff (and an end-to-end case), because each side passed alone
  • C. A larger model
  • D. Fewer tests

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adding more unit tests on the same pieces.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where in the trace does it fail? What did the model return?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Tolerate/normalize the field or enforce a schema.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Seam mismatch; prompt drift; model change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the failing case from the trace.
  5. Root cause: The seam between components was never tested together.
  6. Fix: Constrain output with structured outputs or a schema, add an integration test.
  7. Prevention: Keep traces for every eval run so failures localize to a step.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't rely solely on slow end-to-end tests.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Which level hides most silent failures? → Integration (handoffs).

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more unit tests.
  • Hire: integration test.
  • Strong hire: integration plus schema constraint plus tracing.

questions.promptHtml:
Classify these responses: 429, 529, 400, 401, and a 200 with stop_reason: "refusal".

  • A. All retriable
  • B. 429 and 529 retriable (backoff with jitter, honor retry-after); 400 and 401 terminal; the refusal is terminal and a status-code classifier will not catch it
  • C. 400 retriable, 529 terminal
  • D. Only 429 is retriable

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Ask: would waiting and retrying the identical request plausibly work?

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Retriable: 429, 529, 500, 502, 503, 504. Terminal: 400, 401, 403, 404. A 529 is Anthropic-side load, not a rate-limit signal, and needs a fallback if persistent. When unsure, treat as terminal so the failure is loud. The SDK already retries transient failures, so do not nest your own loop on top (attempts multiply); pick one layer.

questions.promptHtml:
A tool throws an exception. What should the loop return to Claude?

  • A. An empty tool_result
  • B. Nothing; skip the block
  • C. A tool_result with the matching tool_use_id, is_error: true and a clear message, so Claude can react
  • D. A refusal

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. An empty result is treated as valid data and produces a confident, wrong answer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The model treats an empty result as valid data and keeps reasoning on a false premise, producing a confident but wrong answer. Returning is_error: true with a message lets Claude try another approach, ask for clarification or stop. Skipping the block (B) breaks the tool_use/tool_result pairing rule.

questions.promptHtml:
Spend is high and nobody knows why. What is the first step?

  • A. Switch to the cheapest model
  • B. Instrument every call (input tokens, output tokens, latency, error rate) so you can find the one step that accounts for most spend
  • C. Remove all tools
  • D. Disable caching

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Optimizing the wrong step is wasted effort; usually one step is ~90% of the bill.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Then pull the right lever: model routing (default model with an override on a cheap signal such as task type), prompt/context size, number of tool calls, caching for stable prefixes, Batches for non-urgent work (batch discount and caching compound). Define the reliability floor (retry budget, latency ceiling) first and tune cost above it, never below.

questions.contextHtml: A team replaced a single research agent (about 10k tokens per question) with a lead agent plus four parallel subagents. Quality is slightly better; the bill is roughly 15x. Many questions are single-fact lookups.
questions.promptHtml:
What is the best response?

  • A. Keep it; multi-agent is always better
  • B. Route by task: single-fact lookups to one agent, reserve orchestrator-worker for broad, splittable research, and give each subagent its own retry/backoff
  • C. Add more subagents
  • D. Use orchestrator-worker for coding tasks too

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Treating the 15x as acceptable regardless of task shape.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What share of traffic is simple? What is quality vs cost per class?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap fan-out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Over-delegation; oversized tool results per subagent; runaway worker.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-step token logs.
  5. Root cause: Paying for four extra contexts the task did not need.
  6. Fix: B, plus a cheap classifier router.
  7. Prevention: Per-request token budgets and alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't use it for tightly coupled work (coding), where steps depend on each other.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • A worker hits a rate limit with no backoff? → It can stall the lead's synthesis; orchestration multiplies failure handling.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the bill.
  • Hire: routes.
  • Strong hire: routes, bounds fan-out, adds per-worker retries and budgets.

questions.promptHtml:
Which four decisions belong in the pre-code design document?

  • A. Logo, color, name, price
  • B. Success criteria, failure handling (retriable/terminal), cost and latency budget with a reliability floor, and the trust boundary
  • C. Model name, temperature, top_p, top_k
  • D. Team roster and timeline

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Each feeds a later layer: criteria → eval, failures → error handling, budget → instrumentation, trust boundary → hooks and least privilege.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Success criteria become the eval cases; failure handling becomes the retriable/terminal paths; the cost and latency budget (with a reliability floor) becomes what you instrument against; the trust boundary becomes what you treat as data and gate with hooks. Writing them once before building keeps every layer solving the same problem.
